confidence_why: Churchward 1940 (quoted verbatim in McCarthy 2000), Schmidt 2002, Blevins 1994 and Ulfsbjorninn 2019 all put stress on the penultimate syllable in the complete phase and on the final heavy syllable in the incomplete phase, with a long final vowel marking the few lexically final-stressed words; they differ only in analysis (penultimate syllable versus Hayes 1980 and Hale, Kissock and Reiss 2012's penultimate mora, final length underlying or derived), and nearly everything rests on Churchward's single 1940 description with no instrumental study.

sweep_summary: Rotuman (rotu1241) is in the catalog as weight-hedged (Schmidt 2002 deciding; McCarthy 2000 supporting). this search of works with stress in the title found only three title-keyword items, all already listed: Blevins 1994 (Oceanic Linguistics, JSTOR DOI 10.2307/3623138) and two duplicate Glottolog records of McCarthy 2000. McCarthy 2000 (author PDF, already. copied into our files) was re-read: it quotes Churchward 1940 p.75 'the accent falls on the penult' for the complete phase and states that incomplete-phase words all end in a stressed heavy syllable, with final long-vowel words lexically final-stressed -- confirms the catalog on every field and does not supersede Schmidt 2002. Blevins 1994 remains unobtainable open (Semantic Scholar/Unpaywall/OpenAlex/fatcat/author page all closed; it is the primary source of the 'no phonemic length; final stress lexical' analysis the hedge rests on, so it stays high priority for acquisition (Harvard the Harvard library catalogue/JSTOR). Opportunistically downloaded the public-domain JRAI 49 (1919) volume with Hocart's 'Notes on Rotuman Grammar' (not a listed item): it mentions accent only as a conditioning factor for umlaut and gives no stress-placement rule (silent).

new_statements.quote: Stress in Rotuman falls on the penult in complete-phase forms like púre, tokíri, móse, and vá.o. But the accentuation of the corresponding incomplete phase is significantly different. Look first at the treatment of /...VCV/ words: The general rule in the complete phase is that the accent falls on the penult: taka, hili, mose, fora, hanisi, mamosa, hununuka, 'atakoa. (Churchward 1940, p. 75) [T]he stress seems to be levelled out, so to speak, in the inc. phase. Thus: fora becomes foar, which is pronounced almost, though perhaps not quite, as one syllable, the stress being evenly distributed ... (Churchward 1940, p. 86)

new_statements.reading: Complete (citation) phase: stress on the penultimate syllable of all-open-syllable words; final stress only on words with a final long vowel, which McCarthy (following Blevins 1994) treats as lexically final-stressed with length as the reflex. Incomplete phase: the final foot collapses to one heavy syllable, so the word ends in a stressed heavy syllable. Right-edge moraic trochee = 'stress the penultimate mora'. This matches the catalog's weight-hedged coding (right edge, penult default, CVV(+CVC-by-position), phase-conditioned) in every field.

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement and type as the catalog's weight-hedged record (Schmidt 2002: penult in the complete phase, final when the final vowel is long) and as the McCarthy 2000 statement held by the project, which quotes this very p.75 sentence; the first-hand source adds the suffix behaviour (accent stays on the base except -'aki/gerund), the 'every long vowel is accented' link between length and accent, and the per-declension incomplete-phase accent rules (dec.1 keeps accent = final closed syllable, dec.2 level stress).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Complete (citation) phase: word accent on the penultimate syllable; a word ending in a long vowel is accented on the final syllable (and every long vowel carries accent). Suffixation normally leaves the accent where it was in the base (hili > hilia, mose > moseana), except that -'aki and the gerundial suffix (-ga) re-place it on the new penult, and completive -a shifts it in se'ea, vahia. Incomplete phase (p.86): declension 1 (final-vowel elision) keeps the accent on the same vowel, now the final closed syllable (hanisi > hanis); declension 2 (metathesis, fora > foar) has the stress 'levelled out / evenly distributed' over the resulting near-monosyllable; declension 3 (pupui, lelei) shortens the penultimate vowel, accent liable to shift under a following accented word.
new_statements.secondary_stress: No explicit statement of secondary stress; p.73 says every long vowel is accented (so a word may carry more than one accent), and p.86 par.4 notes accent 'liable to be modified by the influence of a following accented word' (phrase level).
new_statements.exceptions: Final accent on words ending in a long vowel (maro, karara with final long vowel); suffixed words keep the base accent (hilia, moseana, jonime, ravatia, fereage) except -'aki and gerundial -ga (penult) and completive -a on se'e, vahi (se'ea, vahia accented on 'e, hi); lexical items flagged in the grammar/dictionary as 'accented on the first syllable' ('atama, fi'ama, 'amtia; utut with two accent patterns); semitama 'without any accent on -ta-', ma 'no accent on either syllable'; incomplete-phase dec.2 forms with levelled stress (foar, mamoas, hununuak).
new_statements.identity_note: Rotuman as spoken on Rotuma (Fiji), described by Churchward from residence 1921-1937; one language, no dialect division made; the 'complete' vs 'incomplete phase' (citation vs phrase-medial forms) is the conditioning the catalog calls phase-conditioned.

readall_conflicts: No new source could be opened, so no new disagreement. Among what is already held by the project for this language there is no conflict on placement: Churchward 1940 p.75 as quoted verbatim in McCarthy 2000 ('The general rule in the complete phase is that the accent falls on the penult'), McCarthy 2000 p.8 ('Stress in Rotuman falls on the penult in complete-phase forms'), and Schmidt 2002 p.817 ('Stress occurs regularly on the penultimate syllable (if the final vowel is short)') all agree on penultimate stress in the complete (citation) phase, with lexically final-stressed words showing a long final vowel, and stress moving to the final (heavy) syllable in the incomplete phase. The only tension is interpretive: Schmidt 2002 p.818 calls Churchward's 'shortening of the penultimate vowel' in /..VV/ incomplete-phase forms 'an awkward statement because the penultimate vowel was not long, but stressed', while McCarthy 2000 p.11 reads the same remark as consistent with a bimoraic-foot analysis; neither changes the placement.

audit.reasoning: Quote check passes: every Schmidt 2002 fragment and the McCarthy 2000 support are verbatim in copies we hold at the stated pages. The deciding source is a 2002 grammar sketch derived from Churchward 1940, backed by two held theoretical phonology papers that transmit Churchward's and Blevins' stress statements; all agree on penult stress in the complete phase, final (heavy) stress in the incomplete phase, and final long vowels co-occurring with final stress. The 'weight-hedged' coding correctly records the genuine analytic split (Hayes/StressTyp2/Hale-Kissock 'penultimate mora' = quantity-sensitive vs Blevins/Schmidt 'penult + lexical final stress realised as length'); Ulfsbjorninn 2019 (downloaded now) sides with Blevins and confirms no instrumental study exists, so no better source is likely to overturn the classification. discovery relied on lingbuzz, Crossref, rotuma.net bi

sources.quote: In the complete phase, words end in open syllables. Stress occurs regularly on the penultimate syllable (if the final vowel is short). If, in exceptional cases, a word is stressed on the final syllable, the final vowel is lengthened in order to attract the accent. The following changes occur in the incomplete phase: (a) If the complete phase ends in CV (where V is unstressed), then this CV > VC, and stress shifts to the final syllable. [...] (b) If the complete phase ends in a stressed vowel (which is phonetically long), then the final vowel is shortened, there is no metathesis, and stress remains on the final syllable. (c) If the word ends in a rising diphthong, there is no deletion or metathesis, but stress shifts to the second vowel of the diphthong.

sources.quote: Each base (major word) in Rotuman has two forms, called 'long' and 'short'. The short form is predictable from the long form, but the reverse is not the case. Long forms are always stressed on the penultimate syllable, short forms on the last syllable. Since forms differing only in the position of stress occur it is considered to be phonemic. e.g. /fáfa/ await /fafá/ challenge. ... A long form is always at least two syllables long. The short form is always one syllable shorter than the corresponding long form. Vowel pairs occur in long forms only, the first vowel of the pair, if stressed, being phonetically long. Each vowel is best considered as being in a different syllable. e.g. /vɔ́i/ [vɔ́:i].

sources.quote: [not read first-hand; as carried by McCarthy 2000, author PDF p.13] Blevins (1994) observes that long vowels have a highly restricted distribution: they are found only root-finally, in native monovocalic roots (rī, rō) and in some polysyllables, mostly loans (sikā, hané 'honey'). ... Words like sikā, Blevins proposes, are represented lexically with an exceptional final stress: /siká/, /hané/. Again, FT-BIN demands bimoraicity. Thus, there is no independent contrast in vowel length, and the restricted distribution of long vowels follows from the restricted distribution of stress.
